title: My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?
summary: A sufferer cries out to a God who seems absent, remembering that Israel's fathers trusted and were delivered while he is mocked, surrounded by enemies pictured as bulls, lions, and dogs, stripped of his clothing, and laid in the dust of death. At the lowest point the prayer breaks off with the declaration that God has answered. The psalm ends in widening praise: in the assembly, among all Israel, to the ends of the earth, among the dead, and to a people not yet born.
story:
Psalm 22 follows two royal psalms in which the king is helped in battle (Psalm 20) and crowned with gold (Psalm 21), and it plunges into the opposite experience: a man abandoned, exposed, and near death. It is followed by Psalm 23, the quiet song of the shepherd who prepares a table in the presence of enemies. The sequence of the crowned king, the forsaken sufferer, and the guest at God's table has struck many readers as deliberate, and it fits the Psalter's larger story, in which the promises to David's line pass through suffering before they are kept.

Psalm 22 is the longest and most developed lament in Book I, and it is the Old Testament passage most woven into the Gospel accounts of Jesus' death. Jesus prayed its first line from the cross, the Gospels tell the crucifixion in its language (the mockers shaking their heads, the taunt that he trusted in God, the soldiers dividing his clothing), and Hebrews puts its turn to praise on the lips of the risen Christ. It is one of the places where the whole Bible's story most clearly bends toward the cross and the resurrection, and it also stands on its own as Israel's fullest prayer for the moment when God seems gone.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘The Doe of the Dawn.’ A Psalm of David.” The first phrase (lamnatseach) appears in fifty-five psalm headings and probably assigns the psalm to the temple's music leader. ‘The Doe of the Dawn’ (ayyelet hashachar) is most likely the name of a melody the musicians knew, now lost; the Septuagint read the words differently as ‘concerning the help that comes at dawn’, connecting them with the rare word eyaluti, ‘my strength’ or ‘my help’, in verse 19. The heading names David, and traditional Jewish and Christian readers have taken him as the author. No episode in David's recorded life matches the psalm closely, which led early Christian readers to say that David spoke here as a prophet beyond his own experience, and led the rabbis to hear other voices in it, notably Queen Esther's (see below).

Modern scholarship classifies the psalm as an individual lament that turns into a song of thanksgiving, following the categories of Hermann Gunkel. Its date is uncertain. Many scholars think the first part (verses 1 to 21) and the thanksgiving (verses 22 to 26) belong to the monarchy or soon after, and some regard verses 27 to 31, with their vision of all nations and even the dead worshiping, as an expansion from the time after the exile, when Israel's hope reached toward the nations (compare Isaiah 45:22-23; Zechariah 8:20-23). Others defend the psalm's unity, pointing out that the praise answers the complaint point by point and that the widening circles of praise are the natural climax of a vow fulfilled. The psalm names no king, battle, or city, and that generality is part of its purpose: any Israelite in mortal danger could pray it, and later Jewish readers applied it to David, to Esther, to the nation in exile, and to the suffering Messiah.

Its images are poetic, not a medical report, but the Gospel writers could see in them the shape of a Roman execution. Crucifixion was the Roman penalty for slaves, rebels, and provincials, carried out in public so that passersby could mock the dying (Mark 15:29). Josephus describes the Romans crucifying so many captives during the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 that there was no room for the crosses (Jewish War 5.451). The only crucified skeleton found in the land of Israel, excavated in 1968 at Givat HaMivtar in Jerusalem and belonging to a man named Yehohanan, still had an iron nail about 11.5 centimeters long through the heel bone, confirming that victims' feet were sometimes nailed. The psalm itself, written centuries before Rome existed, describes being surrounded, exposed, stripped, and left in the dust, and it was that pattern the evangelists recognized.
cultural:
The psalm's enemies are animals from Israel's world. Bashan, the high plateau east of the Sea of Galilee (the modern Golan and the Hauran), was famous for rich pasture, oaks, and fattened cattle (Deuteronomy 32:14; Amos 4:1; Ezekiel 39:18), so its bulls are powerful, well fed, and menacing. It had been the kingdom of Og, whom Israel defeated (Numbers 21:33-35), and in later poetry it stands for arrogant strength. Lions still lived in the Jordan thickets in biblical times (Jeremiah 49:19). Dogs were not household pets but half-wild scavengers that roamed the edges of towns in packs and fed on refuse and the unburied dead (1 Kings 14:11; 21:23-24), and calling someone a dog was a deep insult (1 Samuel 17:43). The reem of verse 21 was the aurochs, the great wild ox of the ancient Near East, now extinct, which Assyrian kings boasted of hunting; the Septuagint translated it monokeros, ‘one-horned’, and so the King James Version has ‘unicorns’.

The body imagery draws on everyday objects. Water poured on the ground cannot be gathered up again (2 Samuel 14:14). Wax melts near a fire (Psalm 68:2). A potsherd is a broken fragment of a clay pot, the driest and most worthless thing in a house, used for scraping (Job 2:8). The mockers ‘part the lip’ and ‘shake the head’, gestures of scorn found also in Lamentations 2:15 and in the Gospels. Dividing a victim's clothing was a practical custom: garments were valuable, and those who had power over a dying man claimed them. The sufferer's memory of birth pictures God as a midwife who drew him from the womb and laid him at the breast; the phrase ‘cast upon you from birth’ may reflect the custom of placing a newborn on the knees of the one who accepted it as his own (Genesis 50:23; Job 3:12).

The second half of the psalm reflects Israel's worship. A person in danger often made a vow (neder), a promise to offer a sacrifice if God delivered him (Jonah 2:9; Psalm 66:13-15). When the rescue came, he paid the vow at the sanctuary with a peace offering, and the law required the meat of such offerings to be eaten by the worshiper and his guests within two days (Leviticus 7:16-18); the related thank offering (todah) had to be eaten the same day (Leviticus 7:11-15). So when verse 26 says “The poor will eat and be satisfied,” it pictures the rescued sufferer hosting a feast of thanksgiving at which the poor are guests. Qahal, the assembly in verses 22 and 25, is the gathered worshiping people of Israel; the ‘great assembly’ may be one of the pilgrimage festivals, when crowds filled the temple courts.
literary:
The psalm is built in two great movements, a lament (verses 1 to 21) and a thanksgiving (verses 22 to 31), joined at a single hinge. Claus Westermann (Praise and Lament in the Psalms, English edition 1981) showed that Israel's laments regularly move from address and complaint through a confession of trust and a petition to a vow of praise, often with a sudden ‘certainty of being heard’. Psalm 22 has every element and stretches each one.

The first movement alternates between complaint and trust, and each time the complaint grows. The cry of forsakenness (verses 1 and 2) is answered by memory: “Yet You are holy,” and our fathers trusted and were not disappointed (verses 3 to 5). The sufferer's shame, “But I am a worm and not a man” (verse 6), and the mockers' taunt (verses 7 and 8) are answered by a second memory, this time personal: you drew me from the womb (verses 9 and 10). Then comes a long complaint without a counterweight (verses 12 to 18), framed by the plea “Be not far from me” (verse 11) and “But You, O LORD, be not far off” (verse 19), which takes up the word ‘far’ from verse 1. The enemies close in as bulls (verse 12), lions (verse 13), and dogs (verse 16), and the rescue plea names them in reverse order: dogs (verse 20), lion and wild oxen (verse 21). Between the animals the body itself comes apart: poured out, disjointed, melted, dried up, laid in the dust, counted, stripped.

The hinge is in the middle of verse 21. The Hebrew runs, ‘save me from the lion's mouth, and from the horns of wild oxen you have answered me’, switching from plea to report in a single line; the BSB marks the break with “You have answered me!” The psalm never says what happened. It records only that God answered, and everything after is praise.

The second movement moves outward in widening circles: my brothers and the assembly (verse 22), all the offspring of Jacob and Israel (verse 23), the great assembly and the poor at the vow meal (verses 25 and 26), all the ends of the earth and the families of the nations (verse 27), the rich of the earth and those who go down to the dust (verse 29), and a posterity and a people yet unborn (verses 30 and 31). The words answer the first half deliberately. “Despised by the people” (verse 6) becomes “He has not despised” (verse 24); the God who hid his face (implied in verse 1) “has not hidden His face from him” (verse 24); the cry that went unanswered (verse 2) is heard (verse 24). The verb safar, to count or recount, is used for counting bones in verse 17, for proclaiming God's name in verse 22, and for telling of the Lord to the next generation in verse 30. The psalm begins with the sufferer's birth (verses 9 and 10) and ends with the birth of a people yet unborn (verse 31). Its last word, ‘he has done it’ or ‘He has acted’, ends a prayer that began with ‘why’.

outline.t: Why have you forsaken me? The God who delivered our fathers
Mocked by all, yet held since birth
Surrounded by bulls, lions, and dogs; poured out like water
Be not far off: you have answered me
The nations, the dead, and the unborn will worship

doctrines.note: The psalm gives the faithful words for the experience of God's absence, and it does not hurry past the complaint. Its first words hold both sides at once: ‘my God’ is said twice in the same breath as ‘why have You forsaken me?’ Lament in Scripture is not unbelief but faith arguing with God on the basis of who he is (verses 3 to 5) and what he has done (verses 9 and 10).

The sufferer is innocent of any named sin, scorned for his trust (verse 8), and laid in the dust of death with God as the agent (verse 15). The psalm refuses to explain the suffering; it brings it before God and waits for him to answer, and it insists that God has not despised the torment of the afflicted (verse 24).

The New Testament reads the whole passion of Jesus through this psalm, and Jesus made its first line his own. Christians have seen in it the shape of the one who bore the sin of many: forsaken, mocked, stripped, and exposed, yet answered by God, whose suffering becomes the occasion of praise and a feast for the poor.

The turn in verse 21 and the praise that follows move from the dust of death (verse 15) to life in the assembly. Hebrews 2:12 places verse 22 on the lips of the risen Christ, reading the thanksgiving as the song of the one God raised from the dead. The psalm itself says only that God answered; the New Testament says how.

The final verses see all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD and all the families of the nations bowing before him (verse 27), echoing the promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3). One sufferer's rescue becomes the reason the nations worship, and the news reaches “a people yet unborn”.

words.note: Azav, to leave, abandon, forsake, about two hundred times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used of leaving a place or a person (Genesis 2:24, a man leaves father and mother), of Israel forsaking the LORD and his covenant (Deuteronomy 29:25; Jeremiah 2:13), and of God's promise not to forsake his people (Deuteronomy 31:6; Psalm 37:28). The standard lexicons list both the physical sense (to leave behind) and the covenantal one. In verse 1 the perfect azavtani, ‘you have forsaken me’, speaks of the forsaking as a present fact, yet it is addressed to ‘my God’: the question is not whether God exists but why the God who is mine has left me.

Rachoq, far, distant, about eighty times, used of distance in space and in time and of God's seeming absence (“Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?”, Psalm 10:1). It is the thread of the lament: “so far from saving me” (verse 1), “Be not far from me” (verse 11, a related verb), and “be not far off” (verse 19). Verse 11 sets the far God against the near trouble (qarov, ‘near’), and the psalm's turn comes when the one who seemed far is found to have heard.

Yeshuah, salvation, deliverance, rescue, about seventy-eight times, more than half of them in the Psalms. It usually names concrete rescue from enemies, sickness, or death, the act by which God brings someone into a safe and open place, and it is the noun from which the name Joshua (and so Jesus, the Greek form of Yeshua) is built. In verse 1 the sufferer says God is ‘far from my salvation’, and the rest of the psalm waits for that rescue to arrive.

Aryeh, lion, one of several Hebrew words for the animal. It appears in verses 13 and 21 for the enemies' roaring and tearing, and the standard Hebrew text also reads the word, ka'ari, ‘like the lion’, in verse 16, where it gives a line without a verb: ‘like the lion, my hands and my feet’. The Septuagint and several other ancient versions read a verb in the same place, ‘they dug’ or ‘they pierced’, and translations divide (see the text note and the first hard question). The sufferer's own cry in verse 1 is sheagah, a word for a lion's roar: he roars like the beasts that roar at him.

Ani, poor, afflicted, humble, from a root meaning to be bowed down, about seventy-five times, nearly thirty of them in the Psalms. It names people bent low by poverty, oppression, or trouble, and God's special care for them runs through the law (Exodus 22:25-27) and the prophets. Verse 24 grounds the whole turn to praise here: God has not despised “the torment of the afflicted” (enut ani, two words from the same root). A related word, anavim, ‘the poor’ or ‘the humble’, names the guests at the thanksgiving meal in verse 26.

Safar, to count, and in the Piel to recount, tell, or declare, about a hundred times. The verb binds the psalm together: the sufferer can “count all my bones” (verse 17), then vows “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers” (verse 22), and at the end the Lord will be ‘declared’ to a new generation (verse 30). The body that could only be counted becomes a voice that recounts God's deeds, and the story is passed on. The same root gives sefer, a book or written record.

Qahal, assembly, congregation, about 120 times, the gathered people of God, whether for worship, for war, or for judgment (Deuteronomy 9:10, the day of the assembly at Sinai). The Septuagint often renders it ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church, and Hebrews 2:12 quotes verse 22 with that word. In the psalm the ‘band of evil men’ (adah, a different word for a gathered company) surrounds the sufferer in verse 16, and the true assembly receives him in verses 22 and 25.

Neder, vow, about sixty times, a promise made to God, usually in distress, to give or do something if he answers (Genesis 28:20-22; 1 Samuel 1:11). The law treated vows seriously and regulated how they were paid (Leviticus 7:16; Numbers 30; Deuteronomy 23:21-23). In verse 25 the rescued sufferer says “I will fulfill my vows”, and the next verse shows what that meant: a sacrificial meal shared with the poor. Prayers in trouble and praise after rescue belong together.

christ:
No psalm is woven more deeply into the story of Jesus' death, and the Gospels use it in several ways at once.

Jesus prayed its first line from the cross. Mark gives the words in Aramaic, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34), and Matthew gives the first word in a form closer to the Hebrew, Eli, which explains why bystanders thought he was calling Elijah (Matthew 27:46-47). The Aramaic Targum of the psalm uses the same verb, shevaq, that Mark records, so Jesus prays the psalm in the language of his own synagogue. Luke and John do not report the cry, and each gives other last words: Luke has Jesus pray Psalm 31:5, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit” (Luke 23:46), and John has “It is finished” (John 19:30).

The Gospels also tell the crucifixion in the psalm's words. Passersby shake their heads (Mark 15:29; Matthew 27:39, echoing verse 7). The chief priests mock, “He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (Matthew 27:43), in words close to the Septuagint of verse 8. The soldiers divide his garments and cast lots (Mark 15:24; Matthew 27:35; Luke 23:34), and John quotes verse 18 in full, “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing,” reading its two parallel lines as two actions, the dividing of the outer garments into four shares and the lot cast for the seamless tunic (John 19:23-24). When John says that Jesus said “I am thirsty” so that Scripture would be fulfilled (John 19:28), he may have verse 15 in mind, or Psalm 69:21. None of the Gospels quotes verse 16, and the connection between the psalm and the crucifixion does not depend on it.

The New Testament also hears the psalm's second half. Hebrews places verse 22 on the lips of the risen Christ: “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly” (Hebrews 2:12), so that Jesus, having shared flesh and blood and death, is not ashamed to call his people brothers. After his resurrection Jesus sends Mary Magdalene to ‘My brothers’ (John 20:17). Hebrews 5:7 says that in the days of his flesh Jesus offered prayers with loud cries and tears and was heard, which many readers connect with verse 24 (“has attended to his cry for help”), though Hebrews does not cite the psalm there. The final vision of the nations turning to the LORD finds its New Testament counterpart in the mission to the Gentiles.

The honest shape of the link is this. Jewish readers have understood the psalm as the prayer of David, of Israel, or of any righteous sufferer, and Christians agree that it was that first. The New Testament's claim is that Jesus prayed it as its fullest speaker: the righteous sufferer who entered its forsakenness without reserve, was answered in resurrection, and whose rescue brings the ends of the earth to worship. The psalm is not a list of predictions that happen to come true; it is a whole prayer that Jesus lived from its first word to its last.
interpretation:
Rabbinic tradition heard Queen Esther in the psalm. The Babylonian Talmud (Megillah 15b) pictures Esther praying ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ as she went unsummoned into the king's presence, and Yoma 29a explains why she is compared to the dawn, the ‘doe of the dawn’ of the heading. The Midrash on Psalms develops the Esther reading at length, and so the psalm became the psalm of the day for Purim in Sephardic communities and among Ashkenazim who follow the rite of the Vilna Gaon, recited at the close of the morning service. Rashi offered several readings of the heading and applied the psalm to the congregation of Israel in exile, crying to God through the long night. Pesikta Rabbati, an early medieval collection of homilies (chapters 36 and 37), applies lines from the psalm, including the taunt of verse 8 and “my strength is dried up like a potsherd” (verse 15), to the sufferings of the Messiah son of Ephraim, who takes on himself the iniquities of Israel's children: a Jewish reading of the psalm as the suffering of a messianic figure.

Christian interpretation began with the Gospels and spread quickly. Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho (around 155 to 160), quotes the psalm at length and expounds it line by line (chapters 98 to 106) as a prophecy of the passion. Tertullian (Against Marcion 3.19) took ‘they pierced my hands and my feet’ as the special cruelty of the cross. Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms and his Letter 140 read the psalm through his idea of the whole Christ, head and body: Christ spoke the cry of forsakenness in the voice of our weakness, taking our humanity's words into his own mouth. Theodore of Mopsuestia (died 428) did not count this psalm among the few he read as direct prophecies of Christ. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae III, question 47, article 3) explained the forsakenness to mean that the Father did not shield Christ from his persecutors but handed him over to suffering, while inspiring in him the will to suffer for us.

The Reformers pressed the cry harder. Luther's Operationes in Psalmos (1519 to 1521), his fullest work on the Psalms, ends with a long exposition of Psalm 22, dwelling on Christ's real experience of God's absence and judgment. Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555), argued that Christ truly felt himself abandoned under the curse of sin while never ceasing to call God ‘my God’. In modern theology Jürgen Moltmann's The Crucified God (German 1972) made the cry the center of a theology of the cross in which the Son suffers abandonment and the Father suffers the loss of the Son; Thomas Weinandy (Does God Suffer?, 2000) is among those who answer that the suffering belongs to the Son in his humanity and that the Father does not cease to love him. Hartmut Gese (1968) argued that the psalm's movement from lament to a thanksgiving meal shaped the earliest telling of Jesus' death and the church's thanksgiving meal, the Eucharist.

The psalm has long been the Good Friday psalm. The Revised Common Lectionary appoints it for Good Friday in all three years, and verses 23 to 31 for the Second Sunday in Lent in Year B, and in many Anglican, Lutheran, and Catholic churches it is said or sung on Maundy Thursday while the altar is stripped. Bach's St Matthew Passion (1727) sets the cry, ‘Eli, Eli, lama asabthani’, in a recitative in which the halo of strings that accompanies Jesus' words throughout falls silent. Handel's Messiah (1742) sets verses 7 and 8 in Part Two (‘All they that see him laugh him to scorn’ and ‘He trusted in God that he would deliver him’), and Haydn's The Seven Last Words of Our Saviour on the Cross (1787) gives the cry its own slow movement.
text:
Hebrew Bibles count the heading as verse 1, so every verse of this psalm is numbered one higher in Hebrew than in English: English 22:1 is Hebrew 22:2, English 22:16 is Hebrew 22:17, and English 22:31 is Hebrew 22:32. Commentaries and articles that follow the Hebrew therefore discuss ‘Psalm 22:17’ where English readers have verse 16. The Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate number the psalm itself as Psalm 21, because they join Psalms 9 and 10.

Several lines read differently in the ancient versions. In verse 1 the Septuagint adds ‘attend to me’ after ‘O God, my God’, and it reads the second line as ‘far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions’, taking the sufferer's ‘groaning’ as ‘transgressions’. In verse 8 the Hebrew has an imperative, ‘commit (yourself) to the LORD’, spoken in sarcasm; the Septuagint and other versions read ‘he trusted in the LORD’, which the BSB follows. In verse 21 the Hebrew ‘you have answered me’ was read by the Septuagint as ‘my lowliness’, continuing the plea (‘save my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns’), so the sudden turn of the Hebrew disappears in the Greek.

Verse 16 is the most debated. The Masoretic Text reads ka'ari, ‘like the lion’, giving ‘like the lion, my hands and my feet’. A few medieval Hebrew manuscripts read ka'aru or karu, verb forms. The Septuagint, translated by Jewish scholars before the Christian era, reads oryxan, ‘they dug’; the Syriac Peshitta also has a verb, ‘they pierced’; Symmachus and Jerome's translation from the Hebrew read a verb meaning ‘bind’. The Psalms scroll from Nahal Hever (5/6HevPs), copied in the first century AD, has a form that Peter Flint (The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible, 1999, with Martin Abegg and Eugene Ulrich) read as ka'aru, a verb, though other scholars say the faint final letter cannot be read with certainty. Translations therefore differ: ‘they pierced my hands and feet’ (KJV, ESV, NIV, BSB), ‘my hands and feet have shriveled’ (NRSV), and ‘like lions [they maul] my hands and feet’ (NJPS).

In verse 29 many scholars redivide the consonants of the opening words to read ‘surely to him shall bow down all who sleep in the earth’, and the NRSV follows this, giving a picture of the dead joining the worship; the BSB keeps the Masoretic ‘All the rich of the earth will feast and worship’. In verses 30 and 31 the Septuagint divides the lines differently. In the New Testament, some later manuscripts of Matthew 27:35, followed by the King James Version, add a fulfillment formula quoting verse 18; the earliest manuscripts lack it, and it was probably borrowed from John 19:24.

teach.big: When God seems absent, faith may cry out to him with the whole truth of its anguish, because the God who answered the forsaken one, and raised the crucified Jesus, turns one sufferer's rescue into praise that reaches the nations and generations yet unborn.

outline.t: Faith can say ‘my God’ and ‘why have You forsaken me?’ in one breath; lament argues with God on the ground of his holiness and his past faithfulness.
When people scorn a believer's trust, the answer is not to hide the shame but to remember that God has held us from birth.
The psalm gives honest words to being surrounded and undone, body and soul, and it lays even that before God as the one who can act.
Prayer keeps asking until God answers, and the answer can come in the middle of the plea.
The rescued sufferer keeps his vow in public: praise in the assembly and a table where the poor eat and are satisfied.
One person's deliverance becomes the reason the nations turn to the LORD and the next generation hears that he has done it.

teach.pitfalls:
The first misreading turns the psalm into a checklist of predictions and skips the prayer. The psalm is not a riddle that happens to match the crucifixion; it is a lament Jesus entered fully, and preaching that jumps from verse to fulfillment misses what it meant for him, and for any sufferer, to pray it. The second misreading rushes to the end. Teachers eager for the resurrection often hurry past verses 1 to 21, but the psalm spends two thirds of its length in the dark, and that proportion is part of its gift to the church.

Several details are often misused. The ‘worm’ of verse 6 (tola'at) is sometimes preached as the crimson-dye insect that dies giving birth, as a picture of Christ's blood; the word does name that insect in some places, but here it means only lowliness, as in Isaiah 41:14, and the insect lore is not in the text. ‘They pierced my hands and feet’ should not be presented as the undisputed Hebrew reading, since the text is contested, and no Gospel quotes it. The cry of verse 1 should not be preached either as proof that Jesus lost faith (he still says ‘my God’) or as a moment when the Trinity was torn apart; Christian traditions describe the forsakenness differently (see the interpretation), but all confess that the Son's union with the Father was not dissolved. Finally, verse 3's ‘enthroned on the praises of Israel’ is sometimes turned into a technique for summoning God's presence through worship; the line is a confession of who God is, spoken from the depths when praise was the last thing the sufferer could feel.
teach.pastoral: This psalm will press on people in grief, chronic pain, depression, and spiritual darkness, and on survivors of abuse who know what it is to be surrounded by predators. Give them permission to pray it as it stands; many believers have never been told that the Bible contains a prayer that accuses God of absence. Do not diagnose anyone or promise that relief will come quickly, since the psalm itself does not say how long the sufferer waited. Point people to the assembly, where the psalm's own rescue is celebrated, and make sure anyone in danger knows how to reach a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or emergency help.

hard.q: Does verse 16 really say “they have pierced my hands and feet”, or is that a Christian reading imposed on the Hebrew?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the objection comes from Jewish readers and from many textual critics. The standard Hebrew text, the Masoretic Text, reads ka'ari, ‘like the lion’, and it is the reading of nearly all Hebrew manuscripts. Rashi and the medieval Jewish commentators read ‘like a lion (they tear at) my hands and my feet’, and modern Jewish translations do the same (NJPS: ‘like lions [they maul] my hands and feet’). They point out that the lion image fits the psalm, which speaks of lions in verses 13 and 21, and that Isaiah 38:13 uses the same comparison for bones broken by God: “Like a lion He breaks all my bones.” Jewish teachers who answer Christian missionaries, such as Tovia Singer, argue that ‘pierced’ is a Christian alteration of the text, and that the Nahal Hever scroll cannot bear the weight Christians put on it because its final letter is unclear. Kristin Swenson (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2004) proposed reading the Masoretic words as a picture of enemies circling the sufferer's hands and feet like a lion.

The case for a verb is also old and not only Christian. The Septuagint, translated by Jews before the Christian era, reads ‘they dug’ (oryxan), and the Syriac Peshitta and other versions also read a verb; the Masoretic ka'ari leaves the clause without a verb, which is unusual. A few medieval Hebrew manuscripts read ka'aru or karu, and the first-century Psalms scroll from Nahal Hever has been read by Peter Flint and others as ka'aru. The translators of the ESV, NIV, and BSB judge that the ancient versions preserve the sense of the original. Others take the verb to mean ‘bind’ or ‘shrivel’ (as in the NRSV), which is neither the lion reading nor ‘pierced’.

Two things are agreed on all sides. The difference between the readings is one letter (yod or vav), easily confused in Hebrew script, so no one needs to charge the other side with bad faith. And none of the Gospels quotes this verse; the New Testament's use of the psalm rests on its first line, the mockery, and the dividing of garments. The church's reading of Psalm 22 as a psalm of the passion does not depend on how this verse is resolved.

hard.q: Did the Gospel writers build their accounts of the crucifixion out of Psalm 22?
hard.a:
The objection has a long history. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) argued that much of the Gospel story grew out of Old Testament texts believed to be messianic. John Dominic Crossan (The Cross That Spoke, 1988; Who Killed Jesus?, 1995) put the case sharply: the first Christians knew little of how Jesus died, so they searched the Scriptures and turned prophecy into narrative, which Crossan called prophecy historicized rather than history remembered. On this view the head-shaking crowds, the taunt about trusting God, and the lots cast for clothing were written into the story because Psalm 22 said so. Jewish critics add that Christians then pointed to the fulfilled ‘predictions’ as proof, a circle that proves nothing.

Several responses are made. Mark Goodacre (in an essay in The Trial and Death of Jesus, 2006) accepts that the Gospels tell the story in Scripture's language but argues that the process ran the other way: a remembered tradition of the crucifixion was later retold in scriptural words, which he calls tradition scripturalized. Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) similarly treated the psalm's echoes as reflection on traditional reports rather than their source. Other scholars point to details that no one would have invented from the psalm: the cry of forsakenness itself is so hard to reconcile with Christian confidence that Luke and John leave it out, and Mark preserves it in Aramaic with the bystanders' misunderstanding about Elijah. The dividing of a condemned man's clothes fits what is known of executions, and the Givat HaMivtar skeleton (found 1968) shows that Roman crucifixion could involve nails through the feet. And the Gospels do not use the psalm the way invention would predict: they never quote the verse most suited to the cross (verse 16), and they place the psalm's language in the mouths of Jesus' enemies, who are mocking, not fulfilling prophecy.

Christians who hold a high view of Scripture differ on how much the evangelists shaped their accounts. Some, such as Craig Blomberg, argue for close historical reporting; others grant that the evangelists selected and phrased details to show the psalm fulfilled, as John openly does (John 19:24), while holding that the events they describe happened. Readers should notice that the New Testament's main use of the psalm is not a proof from prediction. It is the claim that Jesus made this prayer his own, and that God answered him.

observe: Trace the word ‘far’ through verses 1, 11, and 19. How does the sufferer's plea change each time?
List the animals in verses 12 to 21. In what order do they appear in the complaint, and in what order in the plea for rescue?
Follow the circles of praise in verses 22 to 31. Who is included, from the sufferer's brothers to a people not yet born?
interpret: The sufferer calls God ‘my God’ while asking why God has forsaken him. What does that combination teach about the nature of lament?
The psalm never says how God answered in verse 21. Why might it leave the rescue unexplained, and how does the New Testament fill that silence?
Why does the psalm end its thanksgiving with a meal for the poor and a message to future generations rather than with the sufferer's private relief?
apply: Jesus prayed this psalm from the cross. How does that change the way you pray when God seems far away?
Who around you is surrounded, mocked, or near the dust of death, and how could your praise for God's help include them at the table?
Verses 30 and 31 speak of telling a people yet unborn what God has done. What story of God's help do you want the next generation to hear from you?
